title: Enzymes: Catalysis, Kinetics and Control
summary: Understand how enzymes speed reactions, how their speed is measured, and how cells switch them on and off.

lessons.title: Transition States and How Enzymes Lower Activation Energy

levels.kid:
Imagine you want to roll a ball from one valley into another valley. There is a big hill in between. Most of the time the ball just sits there, because pushing it over the hill is hard work.

Chemical reactions in your body are like that. Molecules need a push to get over the hill. That push is called **activation energy**.

**Enzymes** are special helpers made of protein. They don't push harder. Instead, they dig a tunnel through the hill, so the ball gets across much faster and more easily.

The very top of the hill is the trickiest moment, when old parts are breaking and new parts are forming. Enzymes are shaped to hug the molecule tightly at exactly that moment. That is their secret!
levels.hs:
Every chemical reaction has to pass through an unstable, high-energy arrangement called the **transition state**. In it, old bonds are partly broken and new bonds are partly formed. The energy needed to reach it from the starting molecules is the **activation energy**.

If the activation energy is high, few molecules have enough energy at any moment, so the reaction crawls. An **enzyme** is a biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds a reaction by lowering the activation energy.

Key ideas:
- Enzymes do **not** change the overall energy difference between reactants and products. A reaction that releases energy still releases the same amount.
- So enzymes don't change the **equilibrium**, the final balance of reactants and products. They help you get there faster, in both directions.
- The enzyme comes out unchanged and can be used again.
- The **substrate** (the molecule acted on) binds in a pocket called the **active site**.

The speed-ups are astonishing. **Orotidine 5'-phosphate decarboxylase**, an enzyme that helps make DNA and RNA building blocks, speeds its reaction about 10^17 times. Without it, the reaction would have a half-life of around 78 million years; with it, it takes milliseconds.

The main trick is that active sites are shaped to fit the transition state better than the starting substrate.
levels.college:
Transition state theory treats a reaction as movement along a **reaction coordinate** over a free-energy barrier. The rate constant depends exponentially on the activation free energy (deltaG double-dagger): k is proportional to exp(-deltaG double-dagger / RT). At body temperature, lowering the barrier by about 5.7 kJ/mol speeds a reaction roughly 10-fold, so modest stabilization produces huge rate gains.

Enzymes lower deltaG double-dagger but leave the overall deltaG (and Keq) unchanged, accelerating forward and reverse reactions equally.

**Binding energy is the key currency.** Many weak noncovalent interactions (hydrogen bonds, ionic and van der Waals contacts) between enzyme and substrate release energy. Enzymes are built so these interactions are maximal at the transition state, not the ground state. Linus Pauling proposed this in 1946-48: enzymes are complementary to the transition state.

Strategies enzymes use to lower the barrier:
- **Proximity and orientation**: holding reactants together in the correct geometry, reducing entropy loss.
- **General acid-base catalysis**: side chains like histidine donate or accept protons.
- **Covalent catalysis**: a transient covalent bond forms with the substrate.
- **Metal ion catalysis**: metals stabilize charges or activate water.
- **Electrostatic stabilization**: preorganized charges and an **oxyanion hole** stabilize developing charge.
- **Desolvation**: removing water from the substrate.

**Lock-and-key vs induced fit.** Emil Fischer's 1894 lock-and-key model pictured a rigid match. Daniel Koshland's 1958 induced-fit model says the enzyme changes shape on binding. Hexokinase closing around glucose is a classic example; it excludes water and prevents wasteful ATP hydrolysis.

**Transition-state analogs** are stable molecules that mimic the transition state. Because the enzyme binds the transition state most tightly, these analogs are often extremely potent inhibitors, a principle behind many drugs.
levels.phd:
Rate enhancement is quantified as kcat/kuncat, and catalytic proficiency as (kcat/Km)/kuncat. Wolfenden's measurements of uncatalyzed reactions showed spontaneous half-lives from minutes to over a billion years (phosphate monoester hydrolysis), while enzymatic rates cluster within a far narrower band. OMP decarboxylase achieves about 10^17-fold acceleration and proficiency near 10^23 M^-1. Since proficiency formally equals the inverse of the enzyme's notional dissociation constant for the transition state, the implied K_TS can reach about 10^-23 M, far tighter than any ground-state complex.

This framework explains why transition-state analogs bind so well, though real analogs capture only a fraction of that ideal affinity, because they mimic the stable geometry of a fleeting species imperfectly. Classic examples: adenosine deaminase and the analog coformycin; Schramm's picomolar-to-femtomolar immucillins for purine nucleoside phosphorylase, designed from kinetic isotope effect maps of transition-state structure. Lerner and Schultz's catalytic antibodies (1986), raised against phosphonate analogs, validated Pauling's idea but reached only about 10^3-10^6 accelerations, showing complementarity alone is insufficient.

**Jencks' Circe effect**: favorable binding energy is spent to pay for destabilizing the substrate, through strain, desolvation, and loss of translational and rotational entropy. Page and Jencks estimated that freezing out entropy could contribute up to about 10^8 M effective molarity.

**Warshel's electrostatic preorganization** argues the dominant contribution is that the active site dipoles are already oriented to stabilize the transition-state charge distribution, whereas water must reorganize at an energetic cost. Warshel shared the 2013 Nobel Prize partly for QM/MM methods that underpin this view.

Controversies:
- **Ground-state destabilization vs transition-state stabilization**: largely a matter of reference state; what matters is the differential.
- **Near-attack conformers** (Bruice) vs electrostatics.
- **Dynamics**: whether protein motions couple directly to barrier crossing. Hydrogen tunneling, revealed by anomalous temperature dependence of kinetic isotope effects in enzymes like soybean lipoxygenase (KIE about 80), shows classical transition-state theory is incomplete for H-transfer.
levels.expert:
For drug design, transition-state thinking has been commercially decisive. Oseltamivir and zanamivir mimic the oxocarbenium-like transition state of influenza neuraminidase. Many HIV protease inhibitors use hydroxyethylene or hydroxyethylamine isosteres replacing the tetrahedral hydrolytic intermediate. Statins resemble the mevaldyl-CoA intermediate of HMG-CoA reductase. Forodesine (immucillin-H) and the PNP inhibitor ulodesine emerged from Schramm's isotope-effect-guided design; forodesine reached approval in Japan for peripheral T-cell lymphoma. Pentostatin, a coformycin-like adenosine deaminase inhibitor, is used in hairy-cell leukemia.

Practical pitfalls:
- **Tight binding isn't the same as a good drug.** Highly polar transition-state mimics (phosphonates, charged ammonium groups) often have poor permeability and oral bioavailability. Prodrug strategies, like oseltamivir's ethyl ester, address this.
- **Slow-onset, tight-binding kinetics.** Many analogs show time-dependent inhibition. IC50 measured at short preincubation underestimates potency; residence time (1/koff) can predict in vivo efficacy better than affinity alone.
- **Resistance.** Because analogs exploit catalytic residues, resistance mutations often cost the pathogen fitness, but compensatory mutations (seen in HIV protease and neuraminidase H275Y) restore it.
- Kinetic isotope effects reflect the rate-limiting step; if binding or product release limits rate, intrinsic isotope effects are masked and must be unmasked experimentally.

Recent advances:
- **Computational de novo enzymes.** Baker and Houk's "inside-out" theozyme approach (Kemp eliminases, retro-aldolases) initially gave modest rates; directed evolution (Arnold, Nobel 2018) and Hilvert's lab improved Kemp eliminase HG3 to about 10^8-fold acceleration, often by improving preorganization rather than adding new chemistry.
- Deep-learning design (RFdiffusion, 2023-2024 serine hydrolase designs) now generates active sites from scratch, though efficiencies still lag natural enzymes.
- Time-resolved serial crystallography at X-ray free-electron lasers captures intermediates near the transition state.

Open questions: how much evolutionary 'tuning' of conformational ensembles matters, and whether electric field strengths in active sites, measured by vibrational Stark spectroscopy (Boxer), can be a universal design metric.

keyPoints: The transition state is the fleeting highest-energy point of a reaction
Activation energy is the barrier from reactants to the transition state
Enzymes lower the barrier but do not change deltaG or equilibrium
Active sites bind the transition state more tightly than the substrate
Strategies include proximity, acid-base, covalent, metal and electrostatic catalysis
Transition-state analogs make extremely potent inhibitors and drugs

test.q: What is the transition state of a reaction?
choices: The substrate bound in the active site
The stable product formed at the end
The lowest-energy point on the pathway
test.explain: The transition state sits at the top of the energy barrier, with bonds partly broken and partly formed. It is not a stable product or bound substrate.

test.q: How does an enzyme affect a reaction's equilibrium?

It reverses the sign of deltaG
It shifts it toward the reactants
test.explain: Enzymes lower activation energy for forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but its position is unchanged.

test.q: According to Pauling, an enzyme active site is most complementary to:

test.q: Koshland's model in which the enzyme changes shape upon substrate binding is called:

test.explain: Hexokinase is the classic induced-fit example; closing prevents water from hydrolyzing ATP.

test.q: Histidine side chains donating or accepting protons is an example of:
choices: Metal ion catalysis via bound cofactors
test.explain: Proton transfer by side chains such as histidine is general acid-base catalysis.

test.q: Why are transition-state analogs often very potent inhibitors?
choices: They mimic the species bound most tightly
They raise the reaction's activation energy
They change the enzyme's equilibrium constant
They bind covalently to the product
test.explain: Since the active site binds the transition state most tightly, stable mimics of it inherit much of that affinity.

test.q: At body temperature, lowering the activation barrier by about 5.7 kJ/mol speeds a reaction roughly:
test.explain: Rate depends exponentially on the barrier; about 5.7 kJ/mol corresponds to a 10-fold change at 37 degrees C.

test.q: Which enzyme speeds its reaction about 10^17-fold?
test.explain: Orotidine 5'-phosphate decarboxylase is a famous champion, turning a roughly 78-million-year half-life into milliseconds.

test.q: The energy needed to reach the transition state from reactants is the ___ energy.
test.explain: Activation energy is the height of the barrier that enzymes lower.

test.q: What is the name of the pocket on an enzyme where the substrate binds?
test.explain: The active site holds the substrate and stabilizes the transition state.

test.q: A pocket of backbone NH groups that stabilizes developing negative charge on oxygen is the oxyanion ___.
test.explain: The oxyanion hole provides electrostatic stabilization of the transition state.

kidTest.explain: Enzymes are special helpers usually made of protein.

advancedTest.q: If catalytic proficiency is about 10^23 M^-1, what does this imply?
choices: The equilibrium constant is shifted 10^23-fold toward product
The substrate dissociation constant is about 10^-23 M
The enzyme turns over 10^23 substrate molecules per second
The transition state is bound with an implied K near 10^-23 M
advancedTest.explain: Proficiency equals the inverse of the notional transition-state dissociation constant, implying extraordinarily tight transition-state binding, not ground-state binding or a shifted equilibrium.

advancedTest.q: Catalytic antibodies raised against phosphonate analogs gave only modest rate enhancements. The best interpretation is:
choices: Phosphonates raise the activation energy of hydrolysis
Shape complementarity alone lacks preorganized catalytic chemistry
Pauling's complementarity idea is fundamentally incorrect
Antibodies bind small organic molecules too weakly to help
advancedTest.explain: They validated transition-state binding, but natural enzymes also rely on preorganized electrostatics and catalytic groups, so complementarity is insufficient alone.

advancedTest.q: A kinetic isotope effect near 80 for soybean lipoxygenase most strongly suggests:
choices: Product release is the rate-limiting step
advancedTest.explain: Such huge, temperature-anomalous isotope effects exceed the classical limit and indicate H-tunneling, showing classical transition-state theory is incomplete.

advancedTest.q: A transition-state analog shows weak IC50 with brief preincubation but strong efficacy in vivo. A likely explanation is:
choices: Low affinity offset by very high permeability
Rapid metabolism to an inactive compound
Slow-onset binding with a long residence time
Shifting the reaction equilibrium in cells
advancedTest.explain: Many analogs are slow-onset, tight-binding inhibitors; short assays underestimate potency, and long residence time drives in vivo effect.

lessons.title: Michaelis-Menten Kinetics: Km, Vmax and kcat

levels.kid:
Imagine a lemonade stand with one helper. The helper squeezes lemons into lemonade. If only a few lemons arrive, the helper waits around a lot. If more lemons arrive, the helper works faster.

But there is a limit. Once lemons pile up, the helper is busy every second and cannot go any faster. That top speed is called **Vmax**.

Enzymes are tiny helpers in your body. The lemons are like the stuff they work on, called the **substrate**. Some enzymes grab their substrate easily, even when there is only a little around. Scientists measure how easily with a number called **Km**. A small Km means the enzyme is great at finding its substrate. Measuring these numbers tells us how each helper works.
levels.hs:
Enzymes speed up reactions, but how fast do they actually go? **Enzyme kinetics** is the study of reaction speed, and the most famous model comes from Leonor Michaelis and Maud Menten, who published it in 1913.

The enzyme (E) first binds its **substrate** (S) to form an **enzyme-substrate complex** (ES), which then turns into product (P):

E + S ⇌ ES → E + P

Key terms:
- **Initial velocity (v₀)**: how fast product forms right at the start of the reaction.
- **Vmax**: the maximum speed, reached when every enzyme molecule is busy ("saturated").
- **Km (Michaelis constant)**: the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax. A low Km means the enzyme works well even at low substrate levels. Many textbooks call this high "affinity," though that is only roughly true.
- **kcat (turnover number)**: how many substrate molecules one enzyme converts per second when saturated.

If you plot speed against substrate concentration, you get a curve that rises steeply and then levels off. This shape is called a **hyperbola**.

Real example: **carbonic anhydrase**, which turns CO₂ into bicarbonate in your red blood cells, has a kcat of about a million per second. It is one of the fastest enzymes known, which helps your blood carry CO₂ away from your tissues quickly.
levels.college:
The **Michaelis-Menten equation** describes how initial velocity depends on substrate concentration:

v₀ = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S])

**Derivation assumptions.** In the scheme E + S ⇌ ES → E + P (rate constants k₁, k₋₁, k₂):
- **Steady state** (Briggs and Haldane, 1925): [ES] stays roughly constant during the measurement.
- **Initial rates**: product is negligible, so the reverse reaction can be ignored.
- **[S] ≫ [E]total**: binding barely depletes free substrate.

This gives **Km = (k₋₁ + k₂)/k₁** and **Vmax = kcat[E]total**, where kcat = k₂ in this simple scheme.

**Limiting behavior:**
- When [S] ≪ Km, v₀ ≈ (Vmax/Km)[S]. The reaction is first order in substrate.
- When [S] ≫ Km, v₀ ≈ Vmax. The reaction is zero order in substrate.
- When [S] = Km, v₀ = Vmax/2.

**Km is not simply affinity.** Km equals the dissociation constant Kd (k₋₁/k₁) only when k₂ ≪ k₋₁. Many enzymes break this condition.

**Catalytic efficiency, kcat/Km**, is the best single measure of how good an enzyme is at low substrate. It is the second-order rate constant for free E meeting free S and going on to product. Its upper ceiling is set by diffusion, about 10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹. Triose phosphate isomerase, fumarase and acetylcholinesterase come close to this ceiling and are called **catalytically perfect**.

**Linear plots.** The **Lineweaver-Burk** (double-reciprocal) plot graphs 1/v₀ against 1/[S]. The y-intercept is 1/Vmax, the x-intercept is −1/Km, and the slope is Km/Vmax. It was historically useful but distorts errors, because it magnifies the noisy low-[S] points.

**Physiological example.** Hexokinase I has a Km for glucose around 0.1 mM, so it works near Vmax at normal blood glucose (~5 mM). Liver glucokinase has a much higher half-saturation value (~8 mM), so its rate tracks blood glucose. This lets the liver respond to glucose after meals.
levels.phd:
Michaelis and Menten (1913) assumed rapid equilibrium between E, S and ES. Briggs and Haldane (1925) generalized this with the quasi-steady-state approximation, d[ES]/dt ≈ 0. Segel and colleagues later showed the approximation is valid when [E]total ≪ [S]₀ + Km. When enzyme concentration is comparable to substrate, as for some intracellular enzymes or tight-binding inhibitors, the **Morrison quadratic** or full progress-curve analysis is needed.

**Interpreting the parameters in complex mechanisms.** With added steps (E + S ⇌ ES → EP → E + P), kcat becomes a composite of k₂ and k₃: kcat = k₂k₃/(k₂ + k₃). Km is scaled by the same factor, so Km = Ks·k₃/(k₂ + k₃). Both depend on rate-limiting steps after binding. Chymotrypsin acting on ester substrates is the classic case: acyl-enzyme hydrolysis limits the rate, so kcat and Km change together while kcat/Km reflects only the acylation step. This is why **kcat/Km** is often more mechanistically clean. It depends only on steps up to and including the first irreversible step. It also sets **specificity**: for two substrates competing for one enzyme, the ratio of their rates equals the ratio of (kcat/Km)·[S] for each.

**Diffusion limit and perfection.** Albery and Knowles (1976) argued that triose phosphate isomerase has evolved to the point where substrate encounter limits the rate. Viscosity studies support this: adding viscogens such as sucrose slows kcat/Km in proportion to solvent viscosity. Electrostatic steering, as in superoxide dismutase and acetylcholinesterase, can push apparent association rates above simple Smoluchowski estimates.

**Parameter estimation.** Linearizations (Lineweaver-Burk, Eadie-Hofstee, Hanes-Woolf) distort error structure. Hanes-Woolf ([S]/v vs [S]) is the least biased of the three. Today the standard is **nonlinear least-squares fitting** of the hyperbola, or **global fitting of progress curves** using the integrated rate equation (the Lambert W solution). Substrate concentrations should span roughly 0.2–5 × Km. Otherwise Vmax or Km is poorly constrained, and the two estimates become highly correlated.

**Typical magnitudes.** Across the BRENDA database, Bar-Even and colleagues (2011) found that the median enzyme has a kcat near 10 s⁻¹ and a kcat/Km near 10⁵ M⁻¹s⁻¹. Most enzymes are "moderately efficient," far from the diffusion limit. Secondary-metabolism enzymes tend to be slower than those in central metabolism.
levels.expert:
Michaelis-Menten parameters underpin quantitative pharmacology, but their clinical meaning depends on context.

**Saturable drug metabolism.** Elimination of most drugs runs well below the Km of the metabolizing enzyme, so rate is proportional to concentration: **first-order kinetics** with a constant half-life. Phenytoin (CYP2C9/2C19) and ethanol (alcohol dehydrogenase) operate near saturation at therapeutic or typical levels and follow **zero-order (Michaelis-Menten) kinetics**. For phenytoin, small dose adjustments can produce disproportionate rises in plasma level and toxicity, so changes are made in small steps with level monitoring. High-dose salicylate shows similar nonlinearity. Pharmacokinetic models fit an apparent Vmax and Km per patient.

**Pitfalls in assay data.**
- In vitro Km values are measured in dilute buffer. Cytosol is crowded, metabolites are channeled, and local [S] differs from bulk, so in vivo saturation can differ substantially.
- Many enzymes in vivo work at [S] near or below Km. This keeps flux sensitive to substrate and lets pathways self-adjust.
- An apparent Km from microsomes or hepatocytes must be corrected for nonspecific binding (fu,inc). Otherwise intrinsic clearance (Vmax/Km) estimates are biased, which matters for in vitro-in vivo extrapolation.
- Substrate inhibition, cooperativity (Hill-type curves) and atypical CYP3A4 kinetics break the hyperbola. Forcing a Michaelis-Menten fit gives misleading parameters.

**Genetics and disease.** Missense variants often alter kcat or Km rather than abolishing activity. Some inborn errors involving vitamin-derived cofactors arise from raised Km for the cofactor, which is the rationale for high-cofactor therapy in responsive patients. Variant effect maps (deep mutational scanning) increasingly link genotype to kinetic phenotype.

**Recent advances.** Single-molecule turnover studies (Xie and colleagues, 2006) showed that individual enzymes fluctuate between conformations with different rates. Yet the ensemble still obeys a Michaelis-Menten form, with redefined constants. Machine-learning predictors such as DLKcat and TurNuP estimate kcat from sequence and substrate structure to parameterize genome-scale metabolic models, though their errors remain roughly tenfold.

**Open questions.** How accurately do in vitro kcat values reflect in vivo turnover? Proteomics-based apparent kcat estimates in *E. coli* correlate only modestly with in vitro measurements.

keyPoints: Michaelis-Menten: v₀ = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), a hyperbolic curve
Vmax = kcat × total enzyme; reached when enzyme is saturated
Km is the [S] giving half-maximal velocity; it equals Kd only in special cases
kcat (turnover number) counts substrate molecules converted per enzyme per second
kcat/Km measures catalytic efficiency; its ceiling is set by diffusion (~10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹)
Lineweaver-Burk plots distort error; nonlinear fitting is now standard

test.q: What does Km represent in Michaelis-Menten kinetics?
choices: The maximum rate the enzyme can reach
The substrate concentration giving half of Vmax
The number of active sites per enzyme
The time needed to use up half the substrate
test.explain: Km is the substrate concentration at which v₀ = Vmax/2. Vmax is the maximum rate, a different parameter.

test.q: Vmax is reached when:
choices: Product builds up in the solution
test.explain: At saturation essentially every enzyme is bound to substrate, so adding more substrate cannot raise the rate further.

test.q: What does kcat measure?
choices: The energy barrier of the reaction
The total enzyme added to the assay
Substrate turned over per enzyme per second
How tightly substrate binds to enzyme
test.explain: kcat, the turnover number, is the number of substrate molecules one enzyme converts per second when saturated.

test.q: When [S] is much lower than Km, the reaction rate is:
test.explain: At low [S], v₀ ≈ (Vmax/Km)[S], so the reaction is first order. Zero-order behavior happens at high [S].

test.q: Which quantity best describes an enzyme's catalytic efficiency?
test.explain: kcat/Km combines speed and substrate capture. It is the rate constant for free enzyme and substrate going on to product.

test.q: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the y-intercept equals:
test.explain: The double-reciprocal plot has y-intercept 1/Vmax, x-intercept −1/Km and slope Km/Vmax.

test.q: Why is Lineweaver-Burk analysis considered unreliable for fitting data?
choices: It works for allosteric enzymes alone
test.explain: Taking reciprocals inflates the noisy low-substrate points, distorting the fit. Nonlinear fitting avoids this.

test.q: Liver glucokinase has a much higher half-saturation value for glucose than hexokinase I. The result is that glucokinase:
choices: Has its rate track blood glucose
Works at maximum rate during fasting
Is blocked when glucose is plentiful
test.explain: With a half-saturation value near 8 mM, glucokinase activity rises and falls with blood glucose, letting the liver respond after meals.

test.q: Km equals the dissociation constant Kd only when:
choices: The product binds the enzyme tightly
k₂ is much smaller than k₋₁
test.explain: Km = (k₋₁ + k₂)/k₁, which reduces to k₋₁/k₁ = Kd only if k₂ is negligible compared with k₋₁.

test.q: What is the other name for kcat, the number of substrate molecules one enzyme converts per second?
test.explain: kcat is called the turnover number.

test.q: The ___-state assumption, introduced by Briggs and Haldane, treats [ES] as roughly constant.
test.explain: The steady-state approximation assumes d[ES]/dt ≈ 0 during the initial-rate measurement.

test.q: What shape is the curve of v₀ plotted against [S] for a Michaelis-Menten enzyme?
test.explain: The rate rises steeply and then levels off toward Vmax, tracing a hyperbola.

kidTest.explain: Vmax is the fastest the enzyme can work, when it is busy all the time.

kidTest.explain: Like the lemonade helper, the enzyme is busy every second and cannot go faster.

choices: Slow at converting substrate into product
Prone to unfolding at warm temperatures
kidTest.explain: A small Km means the enzyme works well even when there is only a little substrate.

kidTest.explain: The substrate is what the enzyme changes into a product.

advancedTest.q: For chymotrypsin acting on esters, acyl-enzyme hydrolysis limits the rate. How do kcat, Km and kcat/Km respond?
choices: kcat and Km fall together while kcat/Km reports on acylation
kcat/Km reflects deacylation while Km stays fixed
Km stays equal to Kd while kcat reports on the acylation step
kcat rises and Km falls, so efficiency reports on hydrolysis
advancedTest.explain: A slow step after binding scales kcat and Km by the same factor. kcat/Km depends only on steps through the first irreversible step, which here is acylation.

advancedTest.q: Adding sucrose to raise solvent viscosity lowers an enzyme's kcat/Km proportionally. This best supports the idea that:
choices: Chemical bond breaking is the slowest step
The enzyme follows zero-order kinetics in vivo
Sucrose acts as a competitive inhibitor at the site
Substrate encounter by diffusion limits catalysis
advancedTest.explain: If encounter controls the rate, slowing diffusion with viscogens slows kcat/Km in step. This is the classic test for catalytic perfection.

advancedTest.q: Two substrates compete for one enzyme at equal concentrations. Substrate A has a higher kcat but a much higher Km, so its kcat/Km is lower. Which is processed faster?
choices: Substrate A, because it binds the site less
Substrate A, because its turnover is higher
Substrate B, because it has the higher kcat/Km
advancedTest.explain: With competing substrates, the ratio of rates equals the ratio of (kcat/Km)·[S]. The higher kcat alone does not decide specificity.

advancedTest.q: Why can small dose changes cause large plasma-level rises for phenytoin but not for most drugs?
choices: It is cleared by filtration rather than enzymes
Its enzyme works far below Km, giving first-order kinetics
Its metabolizing enzymes operate near saturation
Phenytoin raises the Vmax of its own enzyme
advancedTest.explain: Near saturation, elimination approaches a fixed maximum rate (zero-order), so extra drug cannot be cleared proportionally and levels climb steeply.

lessons.title: Catalytic Mechanisms: The Serine Protease Story

levels.kid:
Proteins are long chains, like beads on a string. Sometimes your body needs to cut those chains. The cutting tools are special enzymes called **serine proteases**. Your gut uses one called **trypsin** to chop up the food proteins you eat.

These enzymes have a tiny team of three helpers inside them, called the **catalytic triad**. They pass a little push from one to the next, like kids passing a ball in a line. The last helper, named **serine**, grabs the chain and snips it.

The enzyme also has a little pocket that holds the chain in just the right spot, like a hand holding paper steady for scissors. That is why it cuts so fast and so neatly.
levels.hs:
Enzymes speed up reactions, but how do they actually do it? One of the best-studied examples is the family of **serine proteases**, enzymes that cut the **peptide bonds** linking amino acids in proteins. They include **chymotrypsin**, **trypsin** and **elastase** from the pancreas, plus blood-clotting enzymes like **thrombin**.

They are named after a key amino acid, **serine**, in the **active site** (the part of the enzyme where the reaction happens). Serine works with two partners, **histidine** and **aspartate**. Together they form the **catalytic triad**:
- Aspartate holds histidine in the right position.
- Histidine pulls a hydrogen off serine.
- This makes serine's oxygen very reactive, so it can attack the peptide bond.

The enzyme also has an **oxyanion hole**, a spot that stabilizes the negative charge that builds up during the reaction. It also has a **specificity pocket** that decides where the enzyme cuts. Trypsin's pocket has a negative charge at the bottom, so it cuts after the positively charged amino acids lysine and arginine.

The reaction happens in two stages. First the protein is cut and one half stays attached to serine. Then water comes in and releases that half. Without an enzyme, a peptide bond in water can last for hundreds of years. Serine proteases cut one in a fraction of a second.
levels.college:
Serine proteases hydrolyze peptide bonds using a nucleophilic serine activated by a **catalytic triad**: **Ser195, His57, Asp102** (chymotrypsin numbering). They illustrate nearly every major catalytic strategy at once.

**Mechanism (ping-pong, two phases):**
- **Acylation.** His57 acts as a **general base** and pulls the proton from Ser195's hydroxyl. The serine oxygen attacks the substrate's carbonyl carbon, forming a **tetrahedral intermediate**. That intermediate then collapses. His57, now acting as a **general acid**, gives a proton to the leaving amine. The C-terminal fragment departs, and an **acyl-enzyme** (an ester bond to Ser195) remains.
- **Deacylation.** Water enters. His57 activates it as a base. Water attacks the acyl-enzyme, forming a second tetrahedral intermediate, which collapses to release the N-terminal fragment and regenerate free Ser195.

**Catalytic strategies on display:**
- **Covalent catalysis**: the acyl-enzyme intermediate.
- **General acid-base catalysis**: His57 shuttles protons.
- **Transition-state stabilization**: the **oxyanion hole**, formed by the backbone NH groups of Gly193 and Ser195, hydrogen-bonds the negatively charged oxygen of the tetrahedral intermediate.
- **Proximity and orientation**: substrate binding positions the scissile bond precisely.

**Specificity** comes from the **S1 pocket**, which binds the residue on the N-terminal side of the cut (the P1 residue):
- Chymotrypsin: a deep hydrophobic pocket, so it cuts after Phe, Trp and Tyr.
- Trypsin: Asp189 at the base, so it cuts after Lys and Arg.
- Elastase: a pocket narrowed by Val and Thr, so it cuts after small residues such as Ala.

The classic kinetic evidence is **burst kinetics**. With the substrate p-nitrophenyl acetate, chymotrypsin releases a rapid "burst" of p-nitrophenolate, then settles into a slower steady state. The burst shows that acylation is fast and deacylation is rate-limiting.
levels.phd:
Serine proteases are a textbook case of **convergent evolution**. The chymotrypsin fold (two β-barrels) and the unrelated **subtilisin** fold (α/β) independently arrived at the same Ser-His-Asp geometry. Carboxypeptidase Y and the α/β-hydrolases (lipases, acetylcholinesterase, which uses a Ser-His-Glu triad) show the motif yet again. That repetition suggests the triad is a near-optimal chemical solution.

**Site-directed mutagenesis** quantified each residue's contribution. Carter and Wells (1988) mutated subtilisin: replacing the catalytic Ser with Ala lowered kcat roughly 10^6-fold, and removing all three triad residues lowered it only modestly more. Even so, the triple mutant was still about 10^3 to 10^4 times faster than the uncatalyzed reaction, so binding and transition-state stabilization contribute independently of the triad.

**Role of Asp102.** Blow's "charge-relay" model proposed full proton transfer from His to Asp. NMR and neutron diffraction later disfavored it. The current view is that Asp102 orients His57 and stabilizes its positively charged imidazolium in the transition state. A **low-barrier hydrogen bond** (LBHB) between His57 and Asp102, proposed by Frey, Cleland and Kreevoy, remains debated. Warshel argues that **electrostatic preorganization** of the active site, not unusual H-bond energetics, explains most of the catalysis.

**Specificity engineering humbles simple models.** Graf and colleagues showed that mutating trypsin's D189S does not produce chymotrypsin-like specificity. Hedstrom and Rutter found that full conversion also required swapping surface loops 1 and 2 and Tyr172. Specificity therefore depends on dynamics, not only on pocket chemistry.

**Mechanism-based inhibition.** **DFP** (diisopropyl fluorophosphate) phosphorylates only Ser195, not the enzyme's other serines, which identified the reactive residue. **TPCK** alkylates His57 in chymotrypsin, and **TLCK** does the same in trypsin; each works only because the inhibitor mimics the preferred substrate. Natural **serpins** use a suicide mechanism: the protease is trapped at the acyl-enzyme stage while the serpin's reactive loop springs into its β-sheet and distorts the active site. Kazal and Kunitz inhibitors (BPTI) instead bind as rigid substrate mimics that are hydrolyzed extremely slowly.
levels.expert:
The serine protease mechanism matters clinically because many drugs and toxins exploit it.

**Drugs that target the triad or S1 pocket:**
- **Direct oral anticoagulants.** Dabigatran is a reversible thrombin inhibitor whose amidine fills the Asp189 S1 pocket. Rivaroxaban and apixaban inhibit factor Xa. Idarucizumab (an antibody fragment) and andexanet alfa (a decoy Xa) reverse them.
- **Gliptins** (sitagliptin and others) inhibit DPP-4, a serine exopeptidase that inactivates GLP-1. Saxagliptin and vildagliptin form a reversible covalent adduct with the catalytic serine.
- **Covalent-reversible viral protease drugs.** Boceprevir and telaprevir targeted the HCV NS3/4A serine protease through a ketoamide warhead that mimics the tetrahedral intermediate. The SARS-CoV-2 main protease uses a cysteine-histidine dyad instead. Nirmatrelvir's nitrile warhead reflects the same design logic carried over to an analogous nucleophile.
- **Sivelestat** inhibits neutrophil elastase.

**Toxicology.** Organophosphate nerve agents and pesticides phosphorylate the catalytic serine of **acetylcholinesterase**. Oximes such as pralidoxime can reactivate the enzyme only before **aging**, a dealkylation step that makes the adduct permanent. Aging can take minutes with soman, which is why the timing of treatment matters.

**Disease from failed control.** α1-antitrypsin (a serpin) protects lung elastin from neutrophil elastase. The Z allele (Glu342Lys) causes the protein to polymerize in hepatocytes, producing emphysema and liver disease together. Hereditary angioedema results from C1-inhibitor deficiency. Mutations in PRSS1 (cationic trypsinogen), such as R122H, block trypsin autolysis and cause hereditary pancreatitis. Notably, **tissue plasminogen activator** (alteplase, tenecteplase) is itself a serine protease. It is used in acute ischemic stroke, a decision neurosurgeons and neurointerventionalists face alongside thrombectomy.

**Research frontiers.** Activity-based probes with fluorophosphonate warheads profile active serine hydrolases across whole proteomes, as in Cravatt's ABPP work, distinguishing active enzyme from zymogen or inhibitor-bound pools. De novo design remains a stress test: computationally designed Ser-His-Asp hydrolases have often formed the triad in crystal structures yet shown weak activity. Reproducing native rates seems to require preorganized electrostatics and dynamics that current design methods capture only partly. Open questions include how conformational sampling couples to chemistry, and how much of the rate enhancement quantum tunnelling and the energetics of the His-Asp hydrogen bond truly account for.

keyPoints: Serine proteases cut peptide bonds using a Ser-His-Asp catalytic triad
His57 acts as a general base and general acid, shuttling protons
The reaction is two-phase: acylation forms an acyl-enzyme, then water deacylates it
The oxyanion hole stabilizes the tetrahedral intermediate's negative charge
The S1 pocket sets specificity: trypsin (Lys/Arg), chymotrypsin (aromatic), elastase (small)
The triad evolved independently in chymotrypsin and subtilisin, an example of convergent evolution

test.q: Which three residues form the catalytic triad of chymotrypsin?
test.explain: Ser195, His57 and Asp102 make up the triad. Cysteine proteases and other enzymes use different residues.

test.q: What is the main job of His57 in the mechanism?
choices: Forming a covalent bond to substrate
Holding a metal ion in place
Shuttling protons as acid and base
test.explain: His57 removes a proton from Ser195 (acting as a base) and later donates one to the leaving group (acting as an acid). Ser195, not His57, forms the covalent bond.

test.q: What does the oxyanion hole stabilize?
choices: The negative oxygen of the tetrahedral intermediate
The positive charge on the substrate's lysine
The free carboxylate of the released product
test.explain: Backbone NH groups of Gly193 and Ser195 hydrogen-bond the oxyanion, stabilizing the transition state.

test.q: Trypsin cuts after lysine and arginine because its S1 pocket contains:
test.explain: Asp189 pairs with positive Lys/Arg side chains. A hydrophobic pocket describes chymotrypsin, and Val/Thr describes elastase.

test.q: Chymotrypsin prefers to cut after which residues?
test.explain: Its deep hydrophobic S1 pocket fits large aromatic side chains such as Phe, Trp and Tyr.

test.q: The intermediate in which part of the substrate is ester-linked to Ser195 is the:
test.explain: After acylation, the N-terminal fragment of the substrate remains attached to Ser195 as an ester until water releases it.

test.q: The initial 'burst' with p-nitrophenyl acetate shows that:
choices: Histidine is the residue being acylated
The enzyme has two separate active sites
Substrate binding is the slowest step
test.explain: A fast burst of product reflects quick acylation of every enzyme molecule, followed by slower turnover limited by deacylation.

test.q: Which catalytic strategy does the acyl-enzyme intermediate represent?
test.explain: The enzyme forms a temporary covalent bond with the substrate, which defines covalent catalysis.

test.q: Which enzyme belongs to the serine protease family?
test.explain: Thrombin is a clotting serine protease. Pepsin is an aspartic protease, carboxypeptidase A is a zinc enzyme and caspases are cysteine proteases.

test.q: In the second phase of the reaction, ___ attacks the acyl-enzyme to release the product.
test.explain: Activated by His57, water hydrolyzes the ester bond and regenerates free serine.

test.q: What is the name for the pocket that decides where a serine protease cuts (letter-number code)?
test.explain: The S1 pocket binds the P1 residue on the N-terminal side of the bond being cut.

test.q: The negatively charged intermediate formed when serine attacks the carbonyl carbon is called the ___ intermediate.
test.explain: The planar carbonyl carbon becomes four-bonded (tetrahedral), with a negative oxygen sitting in the oxyanion hole.

kidTest.q: What do serine proteases cut?
kidTest.explain: They snip the chains that make up proteins.

kidTest.q: Which serine protease helps digest food in your gut?
kidTest.explain: Trypsin chops up the proteins you eat.

kidTest.q: How many helpers are in the catalytic triad?
kidTest.explain: 'Triad' means three: serine and its two partners.

kidTest.q: What does the enzyme's little pocket do?
kidTest.explain: It holds the chain in just the right spot, like a hand steadying paper for scissors.

kidTest.q: Which helper grabs and snips the chain? s _ _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Serine is the last helper in the line, and the enzymes are named after it.

advancedTest.q: In Carter and Wells's subtilisin study, the triple triad mutant remained about 10^3 to 10^4 times faster than the uncatalyzed reaction. The best interpretation is that:
choices: The uncatalyzed rate was overestimated by a factor of a thousand
The mutations failed, so the triad residues were still intact
Subtilisin switches to a metal-dependent mechanism after mutation
Binding and oxyanion stabilization contribute apart from the triad
advancedTest.explain: Residual catalysis without the triad shows that substrate positioning and transition-state stabilization contribute independently.

advancedTest.q: Converting trypsin to chymotrypsin-like specificity required more than the D189S swap. This suggests that specificity:
choices: Depends mainly on the identity of the triad histidine
Is set by the P1 residue's charge and little else
Depends on surface loops and dynamics beyond the pocket
Is fixed by the enzyme's zymogen activation peptide
advancedTest.explain: Hedstrom showed that loops 1 and 2 and Tyr172 were also needed, so the pocket residue alone does not dictate specificity.

advancedTest.q: Why does organophosphate poisoning respond poorly to oximes given late?
choices: The phosphate group migrates from serine to aspartate
Acetylcholinesterase is replaced by its inactive zymogen
The phosphorylated serine undergoes aging and becomes permanent
Oximes are broken down by the triad histidine over time
advancedTest.explain: Dealkylation (aging) of the serine adduct prevents oxime-driven reactivation, which makes early treatment essential.

advancedTest.q: Warshel's view of the His57-Asp102 interaction differs from the LBHB hypothesis by attributing catalysis mainly to:
choices: Quantum tunnelling of the scissile peptide bond
Electrostatic preorganization of the active site
Full proton transfer from histidine to aspartate
Covalent bonding between Asp102 and the substrate
advancedTest.explain: Warshel argues that a preorganized electrostatic environment, not unusually strong hydrogen bonds, explains most of the rate enhancement. Full proton transfer was the older charge-relay idea.

lessons.title: Cofactors, Coenzymes and the Vitamins Behind Them

levels.kid:
Some enzymes can't work alone. They need a little helper, like a drill that needs a battery before it can spin.

These helpers are called **cofactors**. Some are tiny bits of metal, like zinc or iron, that come from food. Others are special molecules called **coenzymes**, and many of them are built from **vitamins**.

That is why vitamins matter so much. Your body uses vitamin B1 to help turn food into energy. It uses niacin, another B vitamin, to carry tiny energy pieces around inside your cells.

If you don't get enough of a vitamin, the enzymes that need it slow down, and you can get sick. A long time ago, sailors without fresh fruit got scurvy because they lacked vitamin C.
levels.hs:
Many enzymes need a non-protein helper to work. This helper is called a **cofactor**. The protein part alone is the **apoenzyme**. The protein plus its cofactor, ready to work, is the **holoenzyme**.

Cofactors come in two kinds:
- **Metal ions**, such as Zn2+, Mg2+, Fe2+ and Cu2+. Zinc in carbonic anhydrase helps turn CO2 into bicarbonate in your blood.
- **Coenzymes**, which are small organic molecules. A coenzyme held very tightly (sometimes by a covalent bond) is called a **prosthetic group**. Heme in hemoglobin is a prosthetic group.

Most coenzymes are made from **vitamins**, especially the water-soluble B vitamins. Your body can't build these vitamins, so they must come from your diet:
- Niacin (B3) becomes **NAD+**, which carries electrons.
- Riboflavin (B2) becomes **FAD**.
- Pantothenic acid (B5) becomes **coenzyme A**.
- Thiamine (B1) becomes **TPP**.

Coenzymes are often called **cosubstrates** because many are changed during a reaction and then recycled. NAD+ picks up electrons to become NADH, then hands them on elsewhere.

A real example: **pellagra**, caused by niacin deficiency, was widespread in the southern United States in the early 1900s. Joseph Goldberger showed it came from poor diet, not infection.
levels.college:
Coenzymes greatly expand what enzymes can do. The 20 amino acid side chains are poor at redox chemistry, carrying one-carbon groups, or stabilizing carbanions. Coenzymes supply that missing chemistry.

Key vitamin-derived coenzymes and their jobs:
- **Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP, from B1)**: its thiazolium ring forms a carbanion that attacks carbonyls. It is used in decarboxylation of α-keto acids (pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) and in transketolase.
- **FAD/FMN (B2)**: carry one or two electrons. They are usually tightly bound, for example in succinate dehydrogenase.
- **NAD+/NADP+ (B3)**: accept a hydride ion. NAD+ mostly serves catabolism, while NADPH serves biosynthesis and antioxidant defense.
- **Coenzyme A (B5)**: its thiol forms high-energy thioesters such as acetyl-CoA.
- **Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, B6)**: forms a Schiff base with amino acids. It supports transamination, decarboxylation (making GABA, serotonin and dopamine) and racemization.
- **Biotin (B7)**: carries CO2 in carboxylases such as pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase.
- **Tetrahydrofolate (B9)**: carries one-carbon units for making purines and thymidylate.
- **Cobalamin (B12)**: used by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase.

**Metal ions** act in several ways. They can be electrophilic catalysts (Zn2+ makes water more acidic in carbonic anhydrase). They can carry electrons (Fe, Cu in cytochromes). They can shield charges (Mg2+ complexed with ATP is the true substrate of kinases).

The difference between a prosthetic group and a cosubstrate matters. A prosthetic group, like FAD in many flavoproteins, is regenerated on the enzyme. A cosubstrate, like NAD+, leaves the enzyme and is reoxidized by another enzyme.

Fat-soluble vitamins work differently. Vitamin K is a true coenzyme for γ-glutamyl carboxylase, which activates clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. Vitamins A and D act mostly as hormone-like ligands.
levels.phd:
Coenzyme chemistry is best understood through the reactive group each one provides.

**PLP** is a classic "electron sink." At rest, it is bound to an active-site lysine as an internal aldimine. A substrate amino acid swaps in to form an external aldimine. The protonated pyridine ring then stabilizes a carbanion at Cα. Which bond breaks depends on **Dunathan's stereoelectronic hypothesis**: the enzyme orients the Cα bond to be cleaved perpendicular to the plane of the π system. Because of this, one cofactor can perform transamination, decarboxylation, racemization or β-elimination depending on the protein.

**TPP**: Ronald Breslow showed in 1958 that the thiazolium C2 proton is unusually acidic. The resulting ylide is a nucleophilic carbene-like species that allows umpolung (reversed polarity) chemistry.

**Flavins** are versatile because they move between the oxidized, semiquinone and hydroquinone states. This lets them link two-electron donors like NADH to one-electron acceptors such as iron-sulfur clusters and ubiquinone. The protein environment tunes the flavin's redox potential across hundreds of millivolts.

**Cobalamin** has a Co-C bond with a bond dissociation energy of roughly 30 kcal/mol. Mutases break this bond homolytically to generate a 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical. Methionine synthase instead uses methylcobalamin through heterolytic methyl transfer.

A key metabolic link is the **folate trap**. When B12 is deficient, folate builds up as 5-methyl-THF, which cannot be recycled. Thymidylate synthesis then fails, causing megaloblastic anemia. At the same time, methylmalonyl-CoA accumulates, which is thought to contribute to the myelin damage of subacute combined degeneration.

Evolutionary angle: White (1976) proposed that nucleotide-based cofactors such as NAD, FAD and CoA are molecular fossils of an RNA world. Their ADP "handles" are often bound by the Rossmann fold.

There is also debate about how "free" cosubstrates really are. NAD+/NADH ratios differ between cytosol and mitochondria, and some pathways may channel these cosubstrates between enzymes rather than releasing them.
levels.expert:
Clinically, coenzyme biology shows up as deficiency syndromes, cofactor-responsive genetic disease, and drugs that target cofactor pathways.

**Wernicke encephalopathy** is the textbook neurological emergency. Thiamine loss impairs pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase in highly active regions such as the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal gray. A key pitfall is giving glucose to a malnourished patient before thiamine, because extra glucose flux can deplete the remaining thiamine and trigger or worsen the syndrome. Treatment decisions belong to clinicians and follow local protocols.

**Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy** (ALDH7A1 mutations) causes neonatal seizures that resist standard antiseizure drugs. Accumulated α-aminoadipic semialdehyde and P6C inactivate PLP. Related **PNPO deficiency** needs PLP itself rather than pyridoxine. For a future neurosurgeon, the point is that a refractory seizure can be a cofactor problem.

**Drug-cofactor interactions**:
- **Isoniazid** forms hydrazones with pyridoxal, causing neuropathy and, in overdose, seizures.
- **Methotrexate** inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, which is why folinic acid can bypass the block.
- **Warfarin** inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1). Genetic variants in VKORC1 and CYP2C9 explain much of the variation in response between patients.
- **Nitrous oxide** oxidizes cob(I)alamin and inactivates methionine synthase. This can unmask subclinical B12 deficiency as myeloneuropathy.

**Cofactor-responsive disease**: some patients with inherited defects improve with high cofactor supplementation. Examples include B6-responsive homocystinuria (cystathionine β-synthase), B12-responsive methylmalonic acidemias, and biotinidase deficiency, which is detected by newborn screening. Many such mutations reduce cofactor binding affinity, so raising cofactor levels can partly rescue the enzyme.

**Frontier**: NAD+ biology. NAD+ is consumed, not just recycled, by sirtuins, PARPs and CD38. Tissue NAD+ declines with age, which drove trials of the precursors nicotinamide riboside and NMN. So far, human benefit is modest and inconsistent. Another open question is how flavin and PLP homeostasis is maintained in neurons, where cofactor shortages may contribute to neurodegeneration.

keyPoints: Cofactors are non-protein helpers: metal ions or organic coenzymes
Apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme; tightly bound coenzymes are prosthetic groups
Most coenzymes come from water-soluble B vitamins (B1 to TPP, B2 to FAD, B3 to NAD+, B5 to CoA, B6 to PLP)
Coenzymes supply chemistry amino acids lack: redox, group transfer, carbanion stabilization
Vitamin deficiencies cripple specific enzymes (thiamine causes Wernicke, B12 causes the folate trap)
Drugs like warfarin, methotrexate and isoniazid act through cofactor pathways

test.explain: Niacin is built into NAD+ and NADP+. FAD comes from riboflavin, and CoA comes from pantothenic acid.

test.explain: PLP forms a Schiff base with amino acids, enabling transamination, decarboxylation and racemization.

test.explain: Biotin carries CO2 in carboxylases such as pyruvate carboxylase. Hydride carriers are NAD(P), and CoA carries acyl groups.

test.explain: Zinc acts as an electrophilic catalyst, making bound water more acidic so it can attack CO2.

choices: It forms a Schiff base with lysine
test.explain: Mg2+ complexes with ATP, shielding its negative charges. The Mg-ATP complex is what kinases actually use.

test.explain: Vitamin K-dependent carboxylation activates clotting factors II, VII, IX and X.

test.q: Pellagra results from a deficiency of:
test.explain: Pellagra is niacin deficiency. Goldberger showed it was dietary, not infectious. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy.

test.explain: Thiamine pyrophosphate drives decarboxylation of α-keto acids and transketolase reactions.

test.explain: Coenzyme A's thiol forms high-energy thioester bonds.

test.explain: Coenzymes are organic cofactors. Metal ions are the other kind of cofactor.

kidTest.explain: Cofactors are helpers that let some enzymes work.

kidTest.explain: Vitamins from food are used to make many coenzymes.

advancedTest.q: Why does B12 deficiency cause megaloblastic anemia even when folate intake is normal?
choices: Folate is trapped as 5-methyl-THF and is not recycled
B12 is needed to absorb dietary folate from the gut
Cobalamin is directly required by thymidylate synthase
advancedTest.explain: Without methionine synthase, folate gets stuck as 5-methyl-THF, so less is available for thymidylate synthesis.

advancedTest.q: One PLP cofactor catalyzes transamination in one enzyme and decarboxylation in another. Per Dunathan, the selectivity mainly arises from:
choices: Variation in the metal ion bound to the phosphate group
Covalent attachment of PLP to a different residue each time
Enzyme orientation of the Cα bond perpendicular to the π system
Different oxidation states of the pyridine ring in each enzyme
advancedTest.explain: The protein aligns the bond to be broken with the π system, so it chooses which bond PLP's electron sink cleaves.

advancedTest.q: Why are flavins, rather than NAD+, suited to pass electrons from NADH to iron-sulfur clusters?
choices: Flavins carry a larger number of electrons per molecule than NAD+
Flavins have a fixed redox potential unaffected by protein environment
Flavins have a stable semiquinone, allowing one-electron steps
Flavins diffuse freely between cellular compartments
advancedTest.explain: The semiquinone state lets flavins split a two-electron hydride into single-electron transfers. NAD+ only does two-electron hydride chemistry.

advancedTest.q: Why can high doses of a cofactor rescue some inherited enzyme defects such as B6-responsive homocystinuria?
choices: Mutations reduce cofactor affinity, which higher concentration partly overcomes
Excess cofactor switches on a backup gene for the enzyme
The cofactor replaces the missing protein with its own catalysis
The cofactor acts as an allosteric inhibitor of competing pathways
advancedTest.explain: Many responsive mutations weaken cofactor binding. Raising cofactor levels increases the fraction of enzyme that is active holoenzyme.

lessons.title: Enzyme Regulation: Allostery, Phosphorylation and Zymogens

levels.kid:
Your body has millions of tiny helpers called **enzymes**. They make chemical jobs happen fast. But sometimes a job should stop, like a faucet you turn off when the cup is full.

Cells have three clever ways to control enzymes:
- **A remote button.** A small molecule sticks to the enzyme away from its working spot and makes it speed up or slow down.
- **A little tag.** The cell clips a tiny phosphate tag onto the enzyme to switch it on or off. Later it can take the tag off again.
- **A safety lock.** Some enzymes are made locked up, so they can't do damage. They get unlocked only where they are needed, like in your belly to digest food.
levels.hs:
Cells must turn enzymes on and off quickly, or they would waste energy and make too much of some molecules. Three major strategies do this.

**Allosteric regulation.** An **allosteric** molecule binds the enzyme at a site separate from the active site ("allo" means other). This changes the enzyme's shape and makes it work faster (an **activator**) or slower (an **inhibitor**). A common pattern is **feedback inhibition**: the final product of a pathway shuts down an early enzyme. For example, CTP, the end product of pyrimidine synthesis, inhibits aspartate transcarbamoylase (ATCase), the first committed enzyme of that pathway.

**Phosphorylation.** Enzymes called **kinases** attach a phosphate group from ATP onto the amino acids serine, threonine or tyrosine. **Phosphatases** remove it. The added negative charge reshapes the protein. This switch is reversible, so it can flip within seconds to minutes, often in response to hormones.

**Zymogens.** Some enzymes are made as inactive precursors called **zymogens** (or proenzymes). They are switched on by having part of the chain cut off, which can't be undone. Digestive enzymes like trypsin are made as trypsinogen in the pancreas. They become active only in the small intestine, which protects the pancreas from digesting itself.
levels.college:
Enzyme activity is controlled on different timescales: allostery acts in milliseconds, covalent modification in seconds to minutes, and changes in enzyme amount (gene expression, degradation) over hours. Control usually targets the **committed step**, the first irreversible step unique to a pathway.

**Allostery.** Allosteric enzymes are usually multisubunit and show **sigmoidal** velocity versus [S] curves, not Michaelis-Menten hyperbolas. This reflects **cooperativity** between subunits switching between a low-activity **T (tense)** state and a high-activity **R (relaxed)** state.
- **ATCase**: six catalytic and six regulatory subunits. CTP inhibits it (stabilizing T) and ATP activates it (stabilizing R), which balances pyrimidine and purine supply.
- **Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1)**: inhibited by ATP and citrate, activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.
- **K-type** effectors change apparent Km; **V-type** effectors change Vmax.

**Reversible phosphorylation.** About 500 human protein kinases phosphorylate Ser, Thr or Tyr residues. Phosphatases reverse the change. In the liver, glucagon raises cAMP, which activates **protein kinase A (PKA)**. This sets off a cascade:
- phosphorylase kinase is phosphorylated and activated, and then phosphorylates and activates **glycogen phosphorylase**;
- PKA also phosphorylates **glycogen synthase**, which inactivates it.

The result is coordinated glycogen breakdown, and each step of the cascade amplifies the signal.

**Proteolytic activation.** Zymogens are activated by cleaving specific peptide bonds, which is irreversible.
- **Enteropeptidase** (enterokinase) in the duodenum converts trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin then activates chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase and more trypsinogen.
- The blood clotting cascade is a chain of zymogen activations, ending with thrombin converting fibrinogen to fibrin.
- Because cleavage can't be reversed, these enzymes are shut off by inhibitors such as **pancreatic trypsin inhibitor** or **antithrombin**.
levels.phd:
Two classic models describe allostery. The **Monod-Wyman-Changeux (MWC, 1965)** concerted model treats each oligomer as existing in only two symmetric states, T and R, in equilibrium (constant L = [T]/[R]). Ligands shift the equilibrium by binding one state more tightly, with the ratio c = K_R/K_T. The **Koshland-Némethy-Filmer (KNF, 1966)** sequential model allows subunits to change one at a time through induced fit. Of the two, only KNF can produce negative cooperativity. The modern **ensemble view** (Hilser, Nussinov) treats allostery as a redistribution of pre-existing conformations, including changes in dynamics with no change in average structure.

ATCase is the canonical example. Gerhart and Pardee showed CTP feedback inhibition in 1962. Lipscomb's crystal structures revealed a quaternary T→R transition in which the catalytic trimers move apart by about 11 Å and rotate. The substrate analog PALA locks the enzyme in R. Effectors mainly change the T/R equilibrium rather than chemistry at the active site.

Phosphorylation adds a dianionic group with about 2 negative charges at physiological pH. It acts through electrostatics, the formation of new binding motifs (14-3-3, SH2, FHA domains), or steric blocking. Glycogen phosphorylase, the first regulatory phosphoprotein identified (Krebs and Fischer, Nobel 1992), shows both modes at once. Phosphorylation at Ser14 and allosteric binding of AMP both favor the R state, while glucose and ATP favor T. Kinase cascades can generate ultrasensitivity: Goldbeter and Koshland's **zero-order ultrasensitivity** arises when an opposing kinase and phosphatase are both saturated, producing switch-like responses. Multisite phosphorylation can likewise set thresholds, as with Sic1 in yeast.

Zymogen activation is structural. In chymotrypsinogen, cleavage between Arg15 and Ile16 frees a new N-terminus. The Ile16 α-amino group forms a salt bridge with Asp194, which reorganizes the oxyanion hole and the S1 pocket. The catalytic triad is already present in the zymogen, so activity is limited mainly by a poorly formed substrate-binding site. Autoactivation and positive feedback, as with trypsin and thrombin, make these systems all-or-none.
levels.expert:
Regulatory sites are increasingly important drug targets. Allosteric drugs avoid the conserved active site, which offers better selectivity, and they can tune activity rather than simply blocking it.

- **Asciminib** binds the myristoyl pocket of BCR-ABL1. It is active in chronic myeloid leukemia that has become resistant to ATP-site inhibitors, including the T315I mutation in some settings.
- **Allosteric KRAS G12C inhibitors** (sotorasib, adagrasib) bind covalently in the switch-II pocket of GDP-bound KRAS, trapping it in its inactive state. They overturned the long-held view that KRAS was "undruggable."
- **MEK inhibitors** (trametinib) bind an allosteric pocket next to ATP.
- **IDH1/2 inhibitors** (ivosidenib, vorasidenib) block mutant enzymes that produce the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate. Vorasidenib is brain-penetrant and was approved in 2024 for IDH-mutant low-grade glioma, a case directly relevant to neurosurgical oncology.

A pitfall is **paradoxical activation**: BRAF inhibitors can promote RAF dimerization and activate MAPK signaling in BRAF-wild-type cells, causing cutaneous squamous lesions.

Zymogen biology appears throughout clinical medicine. **Hereditary pancreatitis** arises from PRSS1 gain-of-function mutations (for example R122H, which removes an autolysis site that normally inactivates trypsin) and from SPINK1 loss of function. Premature trypsinogen activation inside acinar cells starts the injury. Fibrinolytics such as alteplase convert the zymogen plasminogen to plasmin. **Andexanet** and **idarucizumab** reverse the newer anticoagulants by binding them rather than by restoring the zymogen cascade. Caspases are zymogens activated by apoptosomes or by inflammasome-driven proximity. **Pro-convertase processing** generates insulin and other peptide hormones.

In the lab, misleading results are common. Phosphospecific antibodies vary in specificity. Phosphatase activity in lysates (block it with inhibitors) erases signals. Stoichiometry matters, since a site that is 2% occupied may be irrelevant. Phosphoproteomics finds over 100,000 sites, but most have no known function, and many may be non-functional "noise."

Open questions include predicting cryptic allosteric pockets (AlphaFold does this poorly, while molecular dynamics and covalent fragment screening help), designing allosteric switches *de novo*, and understanding how intrinsically disordered regions carry regulatory signals.

keyPoints: Allosteric effectors bind away from the active site and shift T/R equilibria
Allosteric enzymes show sigmoidal kinetics and cooperativity, unlike Michaelis-Menten
Feedback inhibition: end products (e.g., CTP) inhibit early committed steps (ATCase)
Kinases add and phosphatases remove phosphate on Ser, Thr or Tyr: fast and reversible
Zymogens are activated by irreversible cleavage (trypsinogen to trypsin by enteropeptidase)
Regulatory sites are drug targets (asciminib, KRAS G12C inhibitors, vorasidenib)

test.q: Where does an allosteric effector bind on an enzyme?
test.explain: Allo means other: allosteric effectors bind a site distinct from the active site and change the enzyme's shape.

test.q: Allosteric enzymes typically give what shape of velocity vs [S] curve?
test.explain: Cooperativity between subunits produces an S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve, unlike the hyperbolic Michaelis-Menten curve.

test.q: CTP inhibiting ATCase is an example of:
test.explain: CTP is the end product of pyrimidine synthesis and inhibits the pathway's first committed enzyme.

test.q: Which amino acids are the usual targets of protein kinases?
test.explain: Kinases attach phosphate to the hydroxyl groups of Ser, Thr and Tyr.

test.q: What enzyme converts trypsinogen to trypsin in the duodenum?
test.explain: Enteropeptidase (enterokinase), a brush-border enzyme of the duodenum, converts trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin then activates the other pancreatic zymogens, including procarboxypeptidase.

test.q: Why are digestive proteases made as zymogens?
choices: To let them pass into the blood
To protect the cells that produce them
test.explain: Keeping them inactive until they reach the intestine prevents the pancreas from digesting itself.

test.q: In liver, glucagon-triggered PKA activity causes glycogen synthase to become:
test.explain: PKA phosphorylates glycogen synthase, which inactivates it, while the cascade activates glycogen phosphorylase.

test.q: Which form of control is the fastest?
test.explain: Allostery acts in milliseconds. Changing enzyme amount takes hours.

test.q: Once a protease zymogen is activated, how is it usually turned off?
test.explain: Cleavage is irreversible, so inhibitors such as antithrombin or pancreatic trypsin inhibitor shut these enzymes down.

test.q: What class of enzymes removes phosphate groups from proteins?
test.explain: Phosphatases reverse the work of kinases.

test.q: An inactive enzyme precursor activated by cleavage is called a ___.
test.explain: Zymogens such as trypsinogen become active when part of the chain is cut off.

test.q: In the MWC model, the high-activity state is called the R, or ___, state.
test.explain: R is relaxed (high activity) and T is tense (low activity).

kidTest.q: What do enzymes do?
kidTest.explain: Enzymes are helpers that speed up chemical reactions.

kidTest.q: What does the cell clip onto an enzyme to switch it on or off?
kidTest.explain: A tiny phosphate tag works like a switch that can be added or removed.

kidTest.q: Why are some belly enzymes made locked up?
choices: So they stay cool inside the stomach
So they break down food much faster
So they won't harm the body early
kidTest.explain: The lock keeps them safe until they reach the place where food is digested.

kidTest.q: A remote-button molecule sticks to the enzyme where?
choices: On top of the food it uses
kidTest.explain: It binds somewhere else on the enzyme and changes how fast it works.

kidTest.q: Tiny helpers that speed up body jobs are called e _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Enzymes are the body's speedy helpers.

advancedTest.q: Which observation favors the KNF model over the MWC model?
choices: Effectors that shift the T/R equilibrium
A sigmoidal curve with a Hill coefficient above one
A symmetric quaternary T to R transition
advancedTest.explain: MWC can only produce positive cooperativity. Sequential (KNF) induced fit can also explain negative cooperativity.

advancedTest.q: Zero-order ultrasensitivity arises when:
choices: Both opposing enzymes are near saturation
Both enzymes work far below saturation
The kinase is saturated but the phosphatase is not
advancedTest.explain: Goldbeter and Koshland showed that saturated, opposing modifying enzymes give switch-like responses.

advancedTest.q: In chymotrypsinogen, the triad is already present. Activation mainly works by:
choices: A new Ile16 terminus pairing with Asp194
Removing a bound copy of trypsin inhibitor
Phosphorylation that opens the active site
advancedTest.explain: The Ile16-Asp194 salt bridge reorganizes the oxyanion hole and the S1 pocket.

advancedTest.q: Asciminib can work in BCR-ABL1 leukemia resistant to ATP-site drugs because it:
choices: Outcompetes ATP with a higher binding affinity
Binds a separate myristoyl regulatory pocket
Activates a phosphatase that targets ABL1
Cleaves the fusion protein to inactivate it
advancedTest.explain: As an allosteric inhibitor, asciminib binds a site away from the mutated ATP pocket.
